newsitem.title: PERU: No Dominican asylum for Peru rebels - Fujimori.
newsitem.headline: No Dominican asylum for Peru rebels - Fujimori.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori said Marxist rebels holding 72 men hostage in Lima were unlikely to accept refuge in the Dominican Republic, but might be willing to go to another country.
"I don't think the Dominican Republic will be acceptable to them (rebels) as a destination," Fujimori said in an interview aired on local television on Sunday.
"It's possible that in a third country at some moment it may be necessary, and so we're talking about that in an informal way," he added in the interview taped on Saturday.
Fujimori flew to the Dominican Republic on Sunday afternoon for a meeting with President Leonel Fernandez. The agenda included talks on the crisis.

Fujimori refused to reveal the names of countries Peru had approached as possible refuges for the 20-odd Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels holding captives at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima for 75 days.

News reports have touted Cuba, Nicaragua or Eastern Europe as possible sanctuaries in a deal to end Latin America's longest hostage siege. Fujimori said he had not spoken to Cuba's President Fidel Castro about asylum for the guerrillas.
Fujimori's trip to the Dominican Republic comes on the eve of an eighth round of face-to-face talks in Lima between the government and rebels on Monday.
Peruvian press speculated the Dominican Republic might offer asylum after Fujimori met the Dominican president on Feb. 5 during a four-hour stopover at Santo Domingo airport.
The Cuban-inspired MRTA is demanding freedom for 400 jailed comrades. Fujimori has rejected the demand but has floated the idea of asylum for the rebels as part of a deal to free their captives.
The hostages include Fujimori's brother, the envoys of Japan and Bolivia, two Peruvian government ministers and two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats.
